 Pennsylvania Launches a Medicare Fraud Hotline as Scammers Target Seniors Before the December 7 Open Enrollment Deadline 
 Pennsylvania has launched a free, confidential hotline for Medicare beneficiaries to report suspected fraud, as scammers target seniors during open enrollment ahead of the Dec. 7 deadline. 
 Healthy Living 
 Pennsylvania Launches a Medicare Fraud Hotline as Scammers Target Seniors Before the December 7 Open Enrollment Deadline
 Published Nov 16, 2026 10:58 PM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 CHARLY TRIBALLEAU | AFP via Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Pennsylvania has launched a toll-free hotline for Medicare beneficiaries to report suspected fraud, as scammers try to take advantage of the busy annual open enrollment period. The Pennsylvania Department of Aging announced the hotline, 877-435-7014, on Nov. 9, according to a state news release .
 The line is staffed Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and calls are free and confidential. It was set up by Pennsylvania Senior Medicare Patrol, the state's branch of a national program that helps beneficiaries prevent, detect, and report Medicare fraud, errors, and abuse.
 For adult children helping an aging parent compare plans before the Dec. 7 deadline, the timing matters. Open enrollment brings a flood of legitimate calls and mail, which gives scammers cover to slip in requests for Medicare numbers and banking details.
 A New Line During a Busy Season
 Medicare open enrollment runs Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. During this period, beneficiaries can join, switch or drop a Medicare Advantage plan or prescription drug coverage, with changes taking effect Jan. 1.
 About 3 million Pennsylvanians are enrolled in Medicare , roughly 23% of the state's population.
 State officials said the hotline is meant to give people a trusted place to report suspicious contacts. Beneficiaries who receive unexpected calls or requests for information can report them through the hotline and can speak with a trained counselor from the state's free Medicare counseling program, called PA MEDI, about their options.
 Dan Milloy, who oversees the PA MEDI program, urged beneficiaries in the release to "be wary of unknown calls, avoid discussing Medicare with strangers." Secretary of Aging Jason Kavulich urged residents who suspect fraud to call the new line.
 Common Scams Targeting Older Adults
 The department warned about unsolicited requests for personal information, such as a Social Security or Medicare number, offers of supposedly free benefits , unexpected calls from strangers, and unsolicited Medicare-related offers.
 A Medicare number can be used to bill for services or equipment a person never received. Fraudulent claims can show up later on statements and create confusion in a person's medical and billing records. Pennsylvania's attorney general has separately warned about a scam in which medical equipment such as oxygen supplies or wheelchairs is mailed to people who never ordered it and then billed to them or to Medicare, according to an attorney general's consumer alert .
 "Scammers often pretend to be Medicare representatives," Mary Bach, an AARP Pennsylvania volunteer who chairs its consumer issues task force, said in an earlier AARP Pennsylvania warning . AARP Pennsylvania has advised beneficiaries to review Medicare Summary Notices closely to confirm dates and services are correct.
 The release did not report how many fraud complaints the state receives each year or how much money Pennsylvania beneficiaries have lost. It also did not say how quickly reports to the hotline will be investigated or referred.
 Older Adults and Caregivers Most at Risk
 Older adults who live alone, have memory problems or are new to Medicare may be the easiest targets, along with people who recently moved or changed plans and are expecting unfamiliar mail. Caregivers who manage a parent's mail or calls can help spot red flags.
 Medicare does not have its own salespeople, and anyone who calls themselves an official Medicare agent while selling coverage is a scammer, according to the Federal Trade Commission, PhillyVoice reported . Beneficiaries should be suspicious of any unexpected call that asks for a Medicare number.
 Financial pressure adds to the risk. Some older adults are looking for lower premiums or extra benefits, which makes offers of free equipment, cash back, or extra coverage more tempting.
 Steps to Take Before Dec. 7
 Beneficiaries should not give a Medicare, Social Security, or bank account number to anyone who calls, texts, or emails unexpectedly. They can hang up and call the plan or Medicare directly using a number from their card or official mail, including 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). Scammers may also send texts or emails that copy plan logos, so a familiar-looking message is not proof it is real.
 Anyone who suspects fraud can call the Pennsylvania Medicare fraud hotline at 877-435-7014. For help comparing plans, the PA MEDI helpline is 1-800-783-7067, available Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Free counseling is also available through the state's 52 Area Agencies on Aging, which operate the PA MEDI program locally.
 Beneficiaries can review Medicare Summary Notices and plan statements each month for services they did not receive. A person who already shared a Medicare number with a scammer can report it through the hotline and ask Medicare about a replacement card.
 Families can also set a simple rule for an older relative: no plan changes over the phone without a second person present. That one step can stop many high-pressure sales attempts. Caregivers who help a parent can also ask Medicare or the plan about being listed as an authorized representative, which allows them to call on the person's behalf.
 Open enrollment closes Dec. 7, though fraud attempts continue year-round. MedicalDaily will report any data the state releases on hotline reports and recovered losses.

 Key Questions Answered
 What is the new hotline number? 877-435-7014, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Calls are free and confidential.
 Who runs the hotline? Pennsylvania Senior Medicare Patrol established it, and the state Department of Aging announced it.
 What scams should seniors watch for? Unsolicited requests for Medicare or Social Security numbers, offers of free benefits, and unexpected calls from strangers.
 When does Medicare open enrollment end? Dec. 7. Plan changes take effect Jan. 1.
 Where can I get free help comparing plans? PA MEDI at 1-800-783-7067 or through a local Area Agency on Aging.
 What if I already gave my Medicare number to a scammer? Report it to the hotline and contact Medicare about a replacement card.
